title: Cognitive Set 05: Installments, Headcount & Logic
description: Tests equal CI installments, race head-starts, factor counting, coordinate area, attrition DI, and deductive puzzles.

questions.question: In a 1,000-metre sprint, runner A beats runner B by 100 metres or 20 seconds. How many seconds does A take to finish the 1,000-metre race?
questions.explanation: Since A beats B by 100 m or 20 s, B takes 20 seconds to run the final 100 m. Thus B's speed = 100 / 20 = 5 m/s, so B finishes 1,000 m in 1000 / 5 = 200 seconds. A finishes 20 seconds earlier: 200 - 20 = 180 seconds.
questions.shortcut: B runs 100m in 20s => B runs 1000m in 200s => A takes 200 - 20 = 180s.

questions.question: A loan of Rs. 12,300 borrowed at 5% per annum compound interest is to be repaid in two equal annual installments. What is the value of each installment?
How many positive factors of N = 2^4 * 3^3 * 5^2 are exactly divisible by 12?
questions.explanation: Factor out 12 = 2^2 * 3^1 from N: N = 12 * (2^2 * 3^2 * 5^2). Every factor of N divisible by 12 corresponds to a factor of 2^2 * 3^2 * 5^2. Number of such factors = (2+1)*(2+1)*(2+1) = 27.
questions.shortcut: Divide N by 12 => 2^2 * 3^2 * 5^2; product of (exponent+1) = 3*3*3 = 27.

questions.question: A beaker holds 40 litres of a 60% acid solution. How many litres of this solution should be drawn out and replaced with an equal volume of a 20% acid solution so that the resulting mixture becomes 45% acid?
questions.explanation: By alligation between 60% solution (kept) and 20% solution (added) to yield 45%: ratio of 60% to 20% = (45 - 20) : (60 - 45) = 25 : 15 = 5 : 3. Thus 3/(5+3) = 3/8 of the 40 L must be replaced => (3/8)*40 = 15 litres.
questions.shortcut: Alligation gives 25:15 = 5:3; fraction replaced = 3/8 of 40 = 15 L.

questions.question: A solid copper sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and drawn into a uniform cylindrical wire of diameter 0.4 cm. What is the length of the wire in metres?
questions.explanation: Radius of wire = 0.4 / 2 = 0.2 cm. Equating volumes: (4/3)*pi*6^3 = pi*(0.2)^2 * L => 288 = 0.04 * L => L = 288 / 0.04 = 7,200 cm = 72 metres.

questions.question: Three independent replica nodes process a request with individual failure probabilities of 0.10, 0.20, and 0.25 respectively. What is the probability that AT LEAST ONE node processes the request successfully?
questions.explanation: Probability that all three nodes fail simultaneously = 0.10 * 0.20 * 0.25 = 0.005. Therefore, P(at least one succeeds) = 1 - 0.005 = 0.995.

questions.question: How many distinct arrangements of all the letters of the word SERVER can be formed such that the two 'R's are NOT adjacent?
questions.explanation: SERVER has 6 letters with 2 E's and 2 R's. Total distinct permutations = 6! / (2! * 2!) = 720 / 4 = 180. Arrangements where both R's are together (treat RR as 1 block, still 2 E's) = 5! / 2! = 60. Valid arrangements = 180 - 60 = 120.

questions.question: A straight line passes through the points (2, 8) and (6, 4). What is the area of the triangle bounded by this line and the two coordinate axes?
questions.explanation: Slope m = (4 - 8) / (6 - 2) = -1. Equation: y - 8 = -1*(x - 2) => x + y = 10. Thus x-intercept = 10 and y-intercept = 10. Area = (1/2) * 10 * 10 = 50 sq units.

questions.question: What was the net percentage growth in headcount from Q1 opening to Q4 closing?
questions.explanation: Q4 closing headcount = 1,200 + 140 - 90 = 1,250. Net growth from Q1 opening (1,000) = (1250 - 1000) / 1000 * 100 = 25%.

questions.question: Six developers P, Q, R, S, T, and U live on floors 1 to 6 of a building (ground = 1, top = 6). P lives on an even-numbered floor below floor 6. Only two people live between P and Q. T lives immediately above U. S lives on an odd floor above Q. R lives below P and does not live on floor 1. If P lives on floor 4, who lives on floor 6?
questions.explanation: P = 4. Two floors between P(4) and Q forces Q = 1. R lives below P(4) and not on floor 1, so R is on 2 or 3. Since S lives on an odd floor above Q(1), S is on 3 or 5; and T immediately above U needs two adjacent free floors. Testing (T, U) = (6, 5) forces S = 3 and R = 2 (satisfying R < 4). Testing (T, U) = (3, 2) leaves no floor below P(4) for R. Hence T lives on floor 6.

questions.question: Statements: (1) All endpoints are authenticated. (2) Some authenticated routes are rate-limited. (3) No rate-limited route is unencrypted. Conclusions: I. Some authenticated routes are encrypted. II. Some endpoints are rate-limited.
questions.explanation: From (2) and (3), the authenticated routes that are rate-limited cannot be unencrypted, meaning they are encrypted (Conclusion I follows). There is no definite overlap forced between endpoints and rate-limited routes (Conclusion II does not follow).
questions.shortcut: Not unencrypted = encrypted; overlap of Authenticated & Rate-Limited proves I.

questions.question: Introducing a guest at a tech meetup, Sneha said, 'He is the only son of my paternal grandfather's only daughter-in-law.' If Sneha's father has no brothers, how is the guest related to Sneha?
questions.explanation: Since Sneha's father has no brothers, Sneha's paternal grandfather has only one son (Sneha's father), whose wife is Sneha's mother (the grandfather's only daughter-in-law). Her only son is Sneha's brother.
questions.shortcut: Grandfather's only daughter-in-law = Sneha's mother => her only son = Sneha's brother.

In a cipher, every vowel (A,E,I,O,U) is shifted +1 and every consonant is shifted -1 in the alphabet. How is QUEUE coded?
questions.explanation: Apply +1 to vowels and -1 to consonants for QUEUE: Q(consonant)->P, U(vowel)->V, E(vowel)->F, U(vowel)->V, E(vowel)->F => PVFVF.
questions.shortcut: Q-1=P, U+1=V, E+1=F => PVFVF.

questions.question: What is the remainder when positive integer n is divided by 6? Statement I: n is divisible by 3. Statement II: When n is divided by 4, the remainder is 3.
options: Both statements I and II together are necessary
questions.explanation: Statement I alone allows n = 3 (rem 3) or n = 6 (rem 0). Statement II alone allows n = 3 (rem 3) or n = 7 (rem 1). Together: n is an odd multiple of 3 (since n ≡ 3 mod 4 implies n is odd). Every odd multiple of 3 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 6 (3, 9, 15, ...). Sufficient together!

questions.question: Point B is 8 km East of A. Point C is 6 km North of B. Point D is 16 km West of C. Point E is 12 km South of D. How far and in which direction is E from A?
questions.explanation: Put A=(0,0). B=(8,0), C=(8,6), D=(-8,6), E=(-8,-6). Distance from A(0,0) to E(-8,-6) = sqrt((-8)^2 + (-6)^2) = 10 km, in the South-West direction.
questions.shortcut: E is at (-8, -6) relative to A => 3-4-5 scaled by 2 = 10 km South-West.

questions.question: Problem: A production REST service suffered a 40-minute outage because an unindexed query locked the primary orders table during peak checkout traffic. Which immediate course of action is MOST sound? I. Add a read-replica routing rule and deploy the missing composite index via an online non-blocking migration. II. Permanently disable all database foreign keys across every microservice.
questions.explanation: Course I directly fixes the root cause (missing index + read load) safely without locking tables. Course II destroys referential integrity globally and does not fix the unindexed query.
questions.shortcut: Online index + read replica solves the root cause safely; dropping all FKs is destructive.

questions.question: A wall clock is set correctly at 8:00 AM on Monday. It gains 4 minutes every 24 hours. What will the true time be when the clock reads 8:08 AM on Wednesday of the same week?
questions.explanation: From Monday 8:00 AM to Wednesday 8:00 AM is 48 true hours (2 days). In 48 true hours, the clock gains 2 * 4 = 8 minutes, so at true 8:00 AM Wednesday the faulty clock reads 8:08 AM.
questions.shortcut: 48 hours = 2 days => +8 minutes gained => faulty 8:08 AM = true 8:00 AM.

questions.question: Complete the analogy: BDF : EGI :: MOQ : ?
questions.explanation: Letter positions: B(2),D(4),F(6) -> E(5),G(7),I(9), which adds +3 to each letter. Applying +3 to M(13),O(15),Q(17) gives P(16),R(18),T(20) => PRT.
questions.shortcut: Each letter shifts +3: M+3=P, O+3=R, Q+3=T => PRT.

questions.passage: Feature flags decouple code deployment from feature release, allowing engineers to merge incomplete work behind runtime toggles. However, teams that treat flags as permanent fixtures accumulate 'conditional sprawl'—nested branches of dead code paths that complicate testing and obscure system state. Mature engineering organizations enforce strict flag lifecycles: every toggle carries an owner, an expiration date, and an automated reminder that triggers cleanup once a rollout reaches 100% traffic.
questions.question: What problem arises when engineering teams leave temporary feature flags indefinitely in a codebase?
options: Deployment pipelines refuse to merge new branches
Runtime toggles prevent gradual rollouts from reaching 100% traffic
Accumulated conditional branches create dead code paths that hinder testing and clarity
Automated reminders delete active production configurations
questions.explanation: The passage explains that permanent flags create 'conditional sprawl'—nested dead code paths that make testing harder and obscure system state.
questions.shortcut: Check the definition of 'conditional sprawl' in sentence 2.

questions.question: Find the grammatical error: 'The database architect whom (A) / the hiring panel believed (B) / had designed the sharding layer (C) / declined the relocation offer. (D)'
questions.explanation: Ignore the parenthetical clause 'the hiring panel believed': the relative pronoun acts as the subject of 'had designed', so it must be nominative 'who', not objective 'whom'.
questions.shortcut: Strip 'the hiring panel believed' => 'who had designed' (subject case = who).

questions.question:
Order P, Q, R, S logically:
P. Connection pooling solves this bottleneck by pre-allocating a reusable cache of warm TCP sockets.
Q. Opening a fresh TCP connection and TLS handshake for every short SQL query adds tens of milliseconds of overhead.
R. Consequently, high-throughput backends treat pool sizing as a first-class tuning parameter.
S. When an API handler finishes its query, it returns the connection to the pool instead of tearing it down.
questions.explanation: Q defines the overhead problem. P introduces connection pooling as the solution ('solves this bottleneck'). S explains the mechanics ('returns the connection to the pool'). R states the practical consequence ('Consequently'). Order: Q-P-S-R.
questions.shortcut: Problem (Q) -> Solution 'this bottleneck' (P) -> Mechanics (S) -> Conclusion (R).

questions.question: Choose the best replacement: 'By next Friday, the DevOps squad [will complete] migrating all twelve microservices to Java 21.'
questions.explanation: The time marker 'By next Friday' indicates completion prior to a future deadline, requiring the future perfect tense: 'will have completed'.
questions.shortcut: 'By + future time' => future perfect ('will have + V3').

questions.question: Fill in the blanks: 'Because log retention laws are ______, auditors demand ______ audit trails that cannot be silently altered.'
questions.explanation: 'Stringent' (strict) laws require 'immutable' (unchangeable) audit trails—matching 'cannot be silently altered'.
questions.shortcut: 'cannot be silently altered' directly defines 'immutable'.

questions.question: Identify the erroneous segment: 'The candidate brought three luggages (A) / to the assessment center (B) / before checking into (C) / the campus guest house. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Luggage' is an uncountable noun in English and does not take a plural '-s'. Use 'three pieces of luggage' or 'three bags'.
questions.shortcut: 'Luggage', 'information', 'advice', 'equipment' never take '-s'.

questions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S coherently:
P. As a result, a single hot key can saturate one shard while seven sibling shards sit nearly idle.
Q. Consistent hashing distributes keys evenly across storage nodes under uniform demand.
R. Adding a small random salt or local read-through cache spreads those burst reads across replicas.
S. Real-world celebrity profiles, however, generate highly skewed read spikes.
questions.explanation: Q sets the baseline (uniform demand). S introduces the contrast ('however... skewed read spikes'). P describes the result ('As a result, a single hot key...'). R gives the mitigation ('those burst reads'). Order: Q-S-P-R.
questions.shortcut: Q (baseline) -> S ('however', skewed spikes) -> P ('As a result', hot key) -> R (mitigation).

questions.question: Select the grammatically sound replacement: 'One of the microservices that [handles] invoice PDFs crashed during peak billing.'
questions.explanation: In 'One of the [plural noun] that [verb]', the relative pronoun 'that' refers to the plural noun 'microservices', so the verb inside the relative clause must be plural ('handle').
questions.shortcut: 'One of the + plural noun + that + plural verb' ('microservices that handle').

questions.question: Manager: 'Team Alpha closed 140 Jira tickets this sprint whereas Team Beta closed only 85, proving Team Alpha delivered significantly more business value.' Which critique best exposes the flaw in the manager's reasoning?
options: Team Alpha uses dark mode in its Jira dashboard while Team Beta uses light mode
Ticket count ignores task complexity; Team Alpha may have split minor UI fixes into dozens of granular tickets while Team Beta shipped complex architectural work
Team Beta held its sprint retrospective on Friday afternoon instead of Monday morning
Both teams push commits to the same Git repository
questions.explanation: Equating raw ticket count with business value ignores ticket granularity and technical complexity—a classic Goodhart's Law fallacy.
questions.shortcut: Challenge the metric: quantity of tickets != complexity or business value.
